abstract: Direct electrochemical reduction of CO 2 to multicarbon products is highly desirable, yet challenging. Here, we present a potentiostatic pulse-electrodeposition of high-aspect-ratio Cu x Au y nanowire arrays (NWAs) as high-performance electrocatalysts for the CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR). The surface electronic structure related to the Cu:Au ratio in the Cu x Au y NWAs could be facilely modulated by controlling the electrodeposition potential and the as-fabricated Cu x Au y NWAs could be directly used as the catalytic electrode for the CO 2 RR. The morphology of the high-aspect-ratio nanowire array significantly lowers the onset potential of the alcohol formation due to the diffusion-induced enhancement of the local pH and CO concentration near the nanowire surface. Besides, the properly adjusted surface electronic structure of the Cu x Au y NWA enables the adsorption of CO and facilitates the subsequent CO reduction to ethanol via the C –C coupling pathway. Owing to the synergistic effect of morphology and electronic structure, the optimized Cu x Au y NWA selectively reduces CO 2 to ethanol at low potentials of −0.5–−0.7 V vs. RHE with a highest Faradaic efficiency of 48%. This work demonstrates the feasibility to optimize the activity and selectivity of the Cu-based electrocatalysts toward multicarbon alcohols for the CO 2 RR via simultaneous adjustment of the electronic structure and morphology of the catalysts. © 2019 Published by Elsevier B.V. and Science Press on behalf of Science Press and Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences

a b s t r a c t
Direct electrochemical reduction of CO 2 to multicarbon products is highly desirable, yet challenging. Here, we present a potentiostatic pulse-electrodeposition of high-aspect-ratio Cu x Au y nanowire arrays (NWAs) as high-performance electrocatalysts for the CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR). The surface electronic structure related to the Cu:Au ratio in the Cu x Au y NWAs could be facilely modulated by controlling the electrodeposition potential and the as-fabricated Cu x Au y NWAs could be directly used as the catalytic electrode for the CO 2 RR. The morphology of the high-aspect-ratio nanowire array significantly lowers the onset potential of the alcohol formation due to the diffusion-induced enhancement of the local pH and CO concentration near the nanowire surface. Besides, the properly adjusted surface electronic structure of the Cu x Au y NWA enables the adsorption of CO and facilitates the subsequent CO reduction to ethanol via the C –C coupling pathway. Owing to the synergistic effect of morphology and electronic structure, the optimized Cu x Au y NWA selectively reduces CO 2 to ethanol at low potentials of −0.5–−0.7 V vs. RHE with a highest Faradaic efficiency of 48%. This work demonstrates the feasibility to optimize the activity and selectivity of the Cu-based electrocatalysts toward multicarbon alcohols for the CO 2 RR via simultaneous adjustment of the electronic structure and morphology of the catalysts.

1. Introduction 1
Efficient electrochemical reduction of CO 2 to chemical feed- 2 stocks in the industry (e.g., CO/syngas, CH 4 , and C 2 H 4 ) or high 3 energy-density and value-added liquid fuels such as methanol 4 (MeOH), ethanol (EtOH), n-propanol (n-PrOH), and formic acid 5 (HCOOH), ideally using renewable energy sources such as solar, 6 wind, and hydropower, has been considered as an intriguing way 7 to close the anthropogenic carbon cycle [1–5] . In order to conduct 8 such CO 2 electroreduction at a high reaction rate and with a high 9 product selectivity under ambient temperature and pressure, high- 10 performance electrocatalysts toward the CO 2 reduction reaction 11 (CO 2 RR) are essentially needed. To date, due to the high thermo- 12 dynamic stability of CO 2 , complexity of the CO 2 reduction process, 13 and the interference of the competing side reactions (e.g., the 14

Despite the high costs, noble metal (e.g., Au, Ag, 19 and Pt) based electrocatalysts have presented outstanding CO 20 selectivity for the CO 2 RR [8–10] . Lu and co-workers reported a 21 nanoporous silver electrocatalyst that could convert CO 2 to CO at 22 a high reduction rate with a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 92% [8] . 23 Zhu et al. showed that CO 2 could be electrochemically reduced to 24 CO over the monodispersed 8 nm Au nanoparticles at −0.67 V (vs. 25 RHE) with a FE up to 90% [9] . Compared to the production of C1 26 products (e.g., CO, CH 4 , and HCOOH), the selective electroreduction 27 of CO 2 to multicarbon products ( ≥C2) of unsaturated hydrocarbons 28 (e.g., C 2 H 4 and C 3 H 6 ) and alcohols (e.g., EtOH and n-PrOH) is 29 much more challenging due to the more complicated reaction 30 pathways involving C –C coupling, and yet is more desired because 31 the industrial synthesis of C2 products is usually more difficult 32 than that of the C1 products [11,12] . To date, the only reported 33

electrocatalysts for the CO 2 RR that could produce multicarbon 34 hydrocarbons or alcohols in considerable amounts are Cu-based 35 materials. The pioneer work by Hori et al. demonstrated that 36 C 2 H 4 , EtOH, and n-PrOH could form on the electropolished Cu 37 foils at relatively negative potentials and high current densities 38 (e.g., −1.1 V vs. RHE and −5 mA cm −2 ) [13,14] . However, such high 39 overpotentials not only reduce the overall energy efficiency of the 40 CO 2 RR but also trigger various competing hydrogenation and C –C 41 coupling reactions, which in turn hamper the product selectivity. 42 Thus, much effort has been devoted into the development of 43 Cu-based electrocatalysts that could convert CO 2 to multicarbon 44 products at low overpotentials and with high product selectivity. Q2 45 It has been reported that the overpotential for the CO 2 RR de- 46 pends on the binding energies of the intermediates of the CO 2 RR 47 on the catalyst surfaces [15,16] . The binding energy of CO, as a key 48 intermediate for the hydrocarbon and alcohol formation, on the 49 Cu-based catalysts is related to the d -electron availability, which 50 could be adjusted by the morphology and electronic structure of 51 the Cu-based catalysts [10,17,18] . Numerous studies have shown 52 that the Cu-based nanostructures derived from the cuprous and 53 cupric oxide/halide precursors could promote the C –C coupling or 54 alcohol production, which is attributed to the enhanced stabiliza- 55 tion of the chemisorbed ∗CO 2 ̇̄ and ∗CO ( ∗ indicates an adsorption 56 state) on the catalyst surface by the low-coordinated sites created 57 during the precursor reduction [17,19–21] . For example, Li et al. re- 58 ported an oxide-derived nanocrystalline Cu catalyst that could se- 59 lectively convert CO to n-PrOH and EtOH with FEs of 10.0% and 60 42.9%, respectively, at relatively low overpotentials [20] . In addi- 61 tion, the Cu-based binary alloys have emerged as promising elec- 62 trocatalysts for the CO 2 RR because their electronic structures could 63 be facilely adjusted by changing the bimetallic variety, composi- 64 tion, and ordering degree to optimize their activity and selectiv- 65 ity toward the CO 2 RR [22,23] . Moreover, Ma et al. demonstrated 66 that CuO nanowire-derived Cu nanowires with different nanowire 67 lengths and densities exhibited different selectivities toward ethy- 68 lene, n-PrOH, ethane, and EtOH during the CO 2 RR [24] . Specifically, 69 the Cu nanowires presented an enhanced selectivity to ethylene 70 (i.e., a C2 product) as the length and density of the nanowires in- 71 creased, which was ascribed to that the increased local pH caused 72 by the nanowire morphology facilitated the formation of C2 prod- 73 ucts through a CO dimerization pathway. 74 Herein, we present directly electrodeposited high-aspect-ratio 75 Cu x Au y nanowire arrays (NWAs) as high-performance electrocata- 76 lysts for the CO 2 RR. The surface electronic structure of the Cu x Au y 77 NWA, which is associated with the Cu:Au ratio, could be facilely 78 controlled by the electrodeposition potential. The properly ad- 79 justed surface electronic structure along with the nanowire array 80 morphology enhance the CO adsorption on the nanowire surface 81 and facilitate the further selective reduction of the adsorbed CO to 82 EtOH via the dimerization of CO. Besides, owing to the nature of 83 electrodeposition, the paths for the electron transfer from the sub- 84 strate (i.e., the current collector) to the Cu x Au y nanowires are guar- 85 anteed, which is an essential feature for electrocatalysis. Thanks to 86 the synergistic effect of nanowire array morphology and surface 87 electronic structure, the optimized Cu x Au y NWA shows outstand- 88 ing EtOH selectivity with a FE of 45% at −0.7 V vs. RHE. 89
2. Experimental 90
2.1. Materials 91
Cupric sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO 4 • 5H 2 O, 98%), gold(III) chlo- 92 ride trihydrate (HAuCl 4 • 3H 2 O, 49% Au basis), and sodium hydrox- 93 ide (NaOH, 98%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Glycine (gly, 94 99.5%), ethylenediamine (en, 99.0%), and potassium bicarbonate 95 (KHCO 3 , 99.5%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent 96
Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). All the chemicals were used as received 97 without further purification. The anodic aluminum oxide mem- 98 branes (AAO DP65-030-50,0 0 0, with pore diameters between 30 99 and 40 nm ( d Avg. = 35 nm) and a pore depth of about 50 μm) were 100 bought from Topmembranes Technology Co., Ltd (Shenzhen, China). 101 Au and Pt foils (99.9%, cut into disks with a diameter of about 102 14 mm and a thickness of about 0.2 mm) were purchased from Ida 103 Technology Co., Ltd (Tianjin, China). 104
2.2. Electrodeposition of Cu x Au y NWAs 105
The electrodeposition of Cu x Au y NWA was carried out in a 106 three-electrode configuration with a piece of gold foil as the work- 107 ing electrode, Ag/AgCl (in saturated KCl solution) as the reference 108 electrode, and a piece of Pt mesh (1 × 2 cm) as the counter elec- 109 trode. A piece of the AAO membrane (used as a template) was 110 tightly stacked on the top of the Au foil and this AAO-masked Au 111 foil working electrode was sealed in a home-made electrode holder 112 (as shown in Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Material) with a cer- 113 tain exposed surface area of 0.985 cm 2 . Before the electrodeposi- 114 tion of Cu x Au y NWA, a thin layer of Au was galvanostatically pre- 115 electrodeposited at the current density of −0.5 mA cm −2 for 20 min 116 in a solution containing 0.02 M HAuCl 4 and 0.1 M ethylenediamine 117 on a CHI440C electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, China) to fill 118 the slight gap between the Au foil and AAO membrane. The so- 119 lution for the electrodeposition of Cu x Au y NWAs contained 0.02 M 120 CuSO 4 , 0.2 M glycine, 2 mM HAuCl 4 , and 10 mM ethylenediamine 121 [25] . The pH of the deposition solution was adjusted to ∼7.3 by 122 using 5 M NaOH solution. The Cu x Au y NWAs with various atomic 123 ratios of Cu and Au (i.e., CuAu, Cu 3 Au, and CuAu 3 NWAs) were fab- 124 ricated by using a potentiostatic pulse-electrodeposition method in 125 the same deposition solution but with different deposition param- 126 eters at 25 °C on an Autolab PGSTAT204 electrochemical worksta- 127 tion (Metrohm). Specifically, in a single cycle of the potentiostatic 128 pulse-electrodeposition of the CuAu NWA, the potential on the 129 working electrode was first set to −0.45 V for 5 s, then the cell was 130 off for 10 s, and subsequently the potential on the working elec- 131 trode was driven to 0.001 V for 0.05 s. These three potential steps 132 were cycled for 3500 times to accomplish the electrodeposition of 133 the CuAu NWA. The Cu 3 Au and CuAu 3 NWAs were also grown by 134 using the potentiostatic pulse-electrodeposition method except for 135 that the first potential on the working electrode was set to −0.5 136 and −0.4 V and the number of the repeating cycles was 30 0 0 and 137 40 0 0, respectively. The Cu x Au y NWAs were fabricated by using the 138 AAO membrane as the sacrificial template, which was removed in 139 1 M NaOH solution after the electrodeposition. For comparison, the 140 Cu 3 Au film was electrodeposited in the same electrolyte at a con- 141 stant potential of −0.5 V. 142
2.3. Physiochemical characterizations 143
The crystalline structures of the samples were studied by X-ray 144 diffraction (XRD, Rigaku D/Max 2500 diffractometer) at a scan rate 145 of 2 °min −1 from the 2 θ angle of 5 ° to 80 ° using Cu K α radiation 146 ( λ= 0.154184 nm). The morphologies of the samples were investi- 147 gated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova NanoSEM230, 148 at an accelerating voltage of 10 kV) and high-resolution transmis- 149 sion electron microscopy (HRTEM, FEI Titan G2 60-300). The con- 150 tent and distribution of Cu and Au in the fabricated Cu x Au y NWAs 151 were measured by the energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) 152 system integrated in the TEM. To prepare the TEM sample, the fab- 153 ricated Cu x Au y NWA was scraped off from the Au substrate, soaked 154 in 1 M NaOH for 30 min to dissolve any possible residual of the 155 AAO membrane, and then washed with deionized (DI) water and 156 ethanol successively for 3 times. Then, the Cu x Au y nanowires were 157 dispersed in 2 mL ethanol under ultrasonication for 60 min and 158

2.4. Electrochemical reduction of CO 2 167
The electrochemical reduction of CO 2 was carried out in an 168 H-type electrochemical cell with 60 mL of electrolyte in the 169 cathodic compartment and 70 mL of electrolyte in the anodic 170 compartment separated by a proton-exchange membrane (Nafion 171 N115, DuPont). The electrolyte was CO 2 -saturated 0.1 M KHCO 3 172 (pH = 6.8). The electrochemical measurements were carried out in 173 a three-electrode configuration with the fabricated Cu x Au y NWA as 174 the working electrode, a piece of Pt mesh as the counter electrode, 175 and an Ag/AgCl electrode (in 3 M KCl solution) as the reference 176 electrode. The potential versus the reversible hydrogen electrode 177 (vs. RHE) was calculated using the following equation: E (V vs. 178 RHE) = E (V vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.210 V + 0.0591 × pH. The electrochem- 179 ical performance of the electrodeposited Cu x Au y NWAs toward the 180 CO 2 RR was evaluated at different potentials (i.e., −0.5, −0.6, −0.7, 181 −0.8, −0.9, and −1.0 V vs. RHE) at room temperature. During the 182 test, high-purity CO 2 (99.999%) was continuously purged into the 183 cathodic electrolyte at a flow rate of 20 mL min −1 quantified by 184 a gas mass flow meter (MT-52). The gas-phase products of the 185 CO 2 RR were quantified by gas chromatography (GC, SHIMADZU 186 GC-2014C) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) 187 and a flame ionization detector (FID), and the liquid-phase prod- 188 ucts were analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, Bruker 189 AV-400) with dimethyl sulfoxide and phenol as the internal stan- 190 dards [26,27] . By repeatedly pulsing these potentials, the CuAu NWA could be electrodeposited. The CuAu 3 and Cu 3 Au NWAs could also be fabricated using the same pulseelectrodeposition method except for that the first potential on the working electrode needs to be set at −0.4 and −0.5 V, respectively, for obtaining the corresponding Cu:Au ratios of 1:3 and 3:1, respectively, in the Cu x Au y NWAs.
XRD was used to investigate the crystalline structures of the as-electrodeposited Cu x Au y NWAs. It is worth mentioning that in order to avoid the interference from the Au foil substrate, the Cu x Au y NWAs samples prepared for the XRD analysis were electrodeposited on Pt foils. As shown in Fig. 2 (a), the XRD patterns of CuAu 3 , CuAu, and Cu 3 Au NWAs all exhibit the characteristic diffraction peaks of Cu and Au metals. The intensity of the Cu and Au diffraction peaks varies in these Cu x Au y NWAs samples, which matches with the corresponding atomic ratio of Cu:Au. Besides, these Cu and Au diffraction peaks slightly shift and the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of these peaks increases compared to the bulk Cu and Au metal, which are commonly seen in nanomaterials and alloys [18,35–37] . The plan-view and cross-sectional SEM images ( Fig. 2 (b), (c) and S4) show that the electrodeposited Cu x Au y NWAs with different Cu:Au ratios have similar morphologies, which are composed of numerous nanowires with a length of about 20 μm and a diameter of about 35 to 40 nm. Due to the high aspect ratio, these Cu x Au y nanowires tend to lean against the adjacent nanowires after the AAO template is dissolved.
The structure and composition of the as-electrodeposited Cu x Au y NWAs were further characterized by HRTEM and EDS. The HRTEM images of the Cu x Au y NWAs ( Fig. 3 (a), (e) and (i)) show lattice fringes with spacings of about 0.206, 0.236, and 1.44 nm, which correspond to the Cu(111), Au(111), and Au(220) planes, respectively. The corresponding selective area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns of the Cu x Au y nanowires (insets in Fig. 3 (a), (e) and (i)) show concentric rings that could attributed to the diffractions of Cu (111), Au (111), and Au(220), indicating that the obtained Cu x Au y NWAs are polycrystalline. These TEM results match well with the XRD result. The EDS mapping analysis ( Fig. 3 (b), (f), and (j)) shows that Cu and Au are uniformly distributed in the

4. Conclusions 445
In this work, high-aspect-ratio Cu x Au y NWAs with different 446 Cu:Au ratios are fabricated via potentiostatic plus-electrodeposition 447 using the AAO membrane as the template. Compared to the Cu x Au y 448 films with the same Cu:Au ratio, the as-fabricated Cu x Au y NWAs 449 exhibit much enhanced selectivity and lower onset potential to- 450 ward the electrochemical reduction of CO 2 to alcohols (i.e., EtOH 451 and MeOH), which could be attributed to the higher local pH 452 and increased CO concentration near the nanowire surface arising 453 from the limited diffusion of OH −, HCO 3 −, and CO by the dense 454 high-aspect-ratio nanowire array. The Cu:Au ratio in the Cu x Au y 455 NWAs could be easily controlled by the electrodeposition poten- 456 tial, which affects the surface electronic structures of the fabri- 457 cated Cu x Au y NWAs. Different surface electronic structures result 458 in different binding strengths toward the intermediates (e.g., CO) 459 on the nanowire surface, which in turn change the activity and se- 460 lectivity of the Cu x Au y NWAs. The optimized Cu x Au y NWAs show 461 a high EtOH selectivity with FEs of 45% to 48% in the potential 462 range of −0.5–−0.7 V with a maximum partial current density of 463 EtOH formation of 1.0 mA cm −2 . This excellent EtOH selectivity 464 could be attributed to the synergistic effect of morphology and 465 electronic structure that enhances the adsorption of CO on the 466 Cu x Au y nanowire surface and facilitate the subsequent reduction 467 of the ∗CO to EtOH via the CO dimerization pathway. Moreover, 468 the direct growth of the electrocatalysts on conducting substrates 469 by electrodeposition guarantees the paths of electron transfer be- 470 tween the substrates and the catalysts, which is benefitial to the 471 electrocatalysis [43,44] . This work provides an inspiration on de- 472 signing and fabricating Cu-based CO 2 electrocatalysts with high se- 473 lectivity for high-valued C2 products. Q3 474

Thus, among these electrodeposited Cu x Au y NWAs, the Cu 3 Au NWA has the highest capability to stabilize both CO ( ∼0.268 eV on Cu 3 Au (111), Table S7) and H but suffers from unsatisfactory CO selectivity [18] , which means that the adsorbed H species (e.g. proton) are easier to be reduced to H 2 with the increase of the reduction potential. Thus, the Cu 3 Au NWA shows the best EtOH selectivity at a relatively low overpotential of −0.5 V, at which the HER is not severe. In contrast, the CuAu 3 NWA has a better CO selectivity than the Cu 3 Au NWA but suffers from weak binding strength toward CO, resulting in a worse EtOH selectivity but better CO selectivity at −0.5 V vs. RHE compared to that of the Cu 3 Au NWA. Furthermore, the CuAu NWA has a Cu:Au ratio between the Cu 3 Au and CuAu 3 NWAs, which has better CO selectivity than the Cu 3 Au NWA while binds CO stronger than the CuAu 3 ( ∼0.467 eV on CuAu (111) and ∼0.833 eV on CuAu 3 (111), Table S7). The proper electronic structure (modulated by the Cu:Au ratio) along with the nanowire morphology of the CuAu NWA facilitate the generation of an enough amount of CO (i.e., an important intermediate for the reduction of CO 2 to EtOH) and the adsorption of the CO on the catalyst surface for the subsequent reduction to higher value-added products such as EtOH. Besides, the CuAu NWA has the lowest charge-transfer resistance (38.8 ) among these three Cu x Au y NWAs (Fig. S7). Therefore, the CuAu NWA exhibits the highest partial current density of EtOH with a high FE of 45% among the fabricated Cu x Au y NWAs.
